questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Value after a transform applied twice
questions.learningObjective: Compute the value produced when a transform is applied twice.
questions.stem: The costing sheet applies a transform that multiplies the running value by 1.5 and rounds it down to the nearest whole number. Starting from 48, what is the value after the transform is applied twice?

options.text: 108, because each application multiplies the running value by 1.5 and truncates it
72, because applying the transform a second time is the same as applying it once
options.misconception: Treats a second application as a repeat of the first step

options.text: 144, because two applications multiply the starting value by the factor twice over
options.misconception: Scales the original value twice instead of the running value

options.text: 96, because the transform squares the value before scaling it
options.misconception: Assumes the transform squares rather than scales the value

questions.explanation: The transform applies to the running value and rounds each time, so 48 times 1.5 gives 72 and 72 times 1.5 gives 108. Scaling the original twice ignores the intermediate rounding, and doubling the answer by hand is not the rule.
questions.hint: Feed each result back into the transform.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Share of records unique on the quasi-identifiers
questions.learningObjective: Explain the re-identification risk carried by rows unique on the quasi-identifiers.
questions.stem: Supplier invoices on the sheet are keyed by postcode, delivery week and order value band. Eighteen invoices are the only ones sharing each of those three quasi-identifiers. Explain what this uniqueness implies about re-identification risk for those eighteen rows.

answer.exemplar: Those eighteen rows are singletons on the combined quasi-identifiers, so a match on the three fields narrows straight to one invoice rather than to a group, and the risk of re-identification is therefore higher for them than for rows sitting in larger equivalence classes. Fields that look harmless on their own can still be dangerous in combination, so the sheet needs either a narrower disclosure, wider generalisation of one field, or a withholding decision for those rows.

questions.explanation: Singletons mean a match on the three fields lands on one row, collapsing the group to one and raising re-identification risk. Fields that look harmless alone become dangerous in combination.
questions.hint: Think about how many rows a match narrows to.

questions.topic: Share of replications inside a stated interval
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the steps for reporting a share of replications inside an interval.
questions.stem: The sheet tracks whether 20 costed dishes were re-costed inside the agreed two-day window, and 12 of them were. Put the steps for reporting that share in the correct order.

options.text: Count the 12 in-window re-costings, divide by the 20 dishes, multiply by 100, then round
Multiply the 12 by 100, divide by the 20 dishes, count the in-window re-costings, then round
options.misconception: Scales the numerator before establishing the ratio

options.text: Divide the 20 dishes by the 12 in-window re-costings, count them, multiply by 100, then round
options.misconception: Inverts the ratio, so the share exceeds one and reads as 167 percent

options.text: Round the in-window count to a whole percent, count the 12, divide by 20, then multiply by 100
options.misconception: Rounds before the ratio exists, so the percentage is misaligned

questions.explanation: The count comes first, then the ratio, then the percentage conversion, with rounding last once the figure exists. Scaling by 100 first or rounding the raw count breaks the twelve of twenty the sheet records.
questions.hint: Count, divide, scale, then round.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the conditions that must hold before consent can be waived.

stimulus.body: A costing sheet records a trial of a new allergen labelling procedure across the brigade. Staff were told only that the observation would cover record-keeping habits, so nobody knew the true topic of the study.

questions.stem: Given that setup, which condition must hold before the chef may rely on a waiver of informed consent for the allergen findings?

options.text: The study must pose no more than minimal risk and the information gained could not be obtained without the waiver
The chef must publish the findings in the costing sheet so the brigade can review them later
options.misconception: Treats publication after the fact as the condition for a waiver

options.text: Every participating chef must sign the sheet after the trial, which repairs the missing consent
options.misconception: Believes later signatures substitute for consent given upfront

options.text: The allergen labels must be sold at a profit, showing the trial caused no commercial loss
options.misconception: Confuses commercial benefit with the risk threshold for a waiver

questions.explanation: A waiver needs no more than minimal risk and information unobtainable without it. Signing later or publishing later does not create the condition, and profit is irrelevant to the risk test.
questions.hint: Two conditions, both about risk and necessity.

Disclose nothing beyond the results, then let staff appeal the session scoring afterwards
options.misconception: Treats the debriefing as a results meeting with an appeal step

options.text: Disclose the deception and the true purpose, then require staff to repeat the tasting
options.misconception: Makes a second trial a condition of a valid debriefing

options.text: Disclose only that a deception occurred, then delete the tasting notes without asking
options.misconception: Treats removing the data as an adequate debriefing

questions.explanation: The debriefing must disclose the deception and its true purpose and offer withdrawal of the participant's data. Repeating the tasting or quietly deleting notes does not remedy the deception or respect the choice.
questions.hint: Tell the truth, then return the choice.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Judge how minimal risk is determined from the facts of a procedure.
questions.stem: The sheet records that the allergen trial exposed 24 staff to a possible irritant with a 1 in 400 chance of causing a mild skin reaction, and every session included protective gloves and a wash station. On these facts, how should minimal risk be judged?

options.text: As minimal, because the chance and severity of harm are low and the safeguards reduce them further
As minimal, because a low probability alone settles the question regardless of the severity
options.misconception: Ignores the magnitude of harm and the protective measures

options.text: As more than minimal, because any physical exposure at all exceeds the minimal threshold
options.misconception: Treats any measurable exposure as automatically above minimal risk

options.text: As minimal, because staff volunteers accept every risk once they sign the costing sheet
options.misconception: Assumes a signed sheet removes the need to weigh probability and severity

questions.explanation: Minimal risk weighs probability and magnitude of harm, with safeguards and context in view. A low probability does not excuse a severe outcome, and a signature never makes exposure harmless.
questions.hint: Judge probability together with severity.

1, because the transform is applied once to the original score and repeated
options.misconception: Treats the second application as a repeat of the first step

questions.topic: Share of records unique on the quasi-identifiers
questions.learningObjective: Explain what uniqueness on the quasi-identifiers implies for protecting a sheet.
questions.stem: The sheet stores supplier invoices for 200 orders and 30 of them are the only records carrying a given postcode, week and value band together. Explain what this 30 out of 200 pattern says about how the sheet would need to be protected.

answer.exemplar: Thirty invoices are singletons on the combined quasi-identifiers, so a buyer holding an external supplier-and-date list could attach a single supplier name to each of those rows, whereas the remaining 170 rows would only ever narrow to a set of suppliers. Protection therefore means treating the 30 singleton rows differently, for instance by removing the exact week, widening the postcode or withholding them, and the decision and its reasoning should be written into the sheet rather than left to whoever extracts the data.

questions.explanation: Singleton rows collapse to a single match each and carry far higher risk than the grouped majority. Averaging risk across all 200 rows and calling the file safe is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Compare the exposed rows with the rest.

That 65 per cent of the costings were reproduced inside the window, with 13 outside
options.misconception: Inverts the share, reporting the misses as the hits

options.text: That 20 costings were all inside the window, since the window is the agreed standard
options.misconception: Assumes agreement of the window means the work met it

options.text: That 7 costings were reproduced exactly, since the others were never attempted
options.misconception: Reads an unsuccessful re-costing as no attempt being made

questions.explanation: The figure counts 7 of 20, so 35 per cent fell inside the window and 13 fell outside, and the two figures together make the record complete. Quoting the complement flips hits into misses while still looking plausible.
questions.hint: The complement is not the share.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a debriefing after deception must achieve.
questions.stem: The sheet records that a plating exercise was used to test whether staff notice a changed garnish, and they were told the garnish was routine. Explain what a debriefing must achieve here and why an apology would not do the same job.

answer.exemplar: A debriefing has to tell the participants that the garnish change was the real focus of the exercise, explain why it was concealed, and restore their choice by letting them withdraw the observations or refuse to have them used. An apology does not do that job because it addresses the feelings of the staff but leaves them in the dark about the deception and in the position that their participation served a purpose they did not choose to support.

questions.explanation: A debriefing must disclose the deception and its real purpose and restore the choice taken away, whereas an apology addresses feelings without telling people what was done to them. Treating regret as disclosure is the error.
questions.hint: Disclosure and restored choice, not regret.

questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for judging whether a risk is minimal.
questions.stem: The sheet describes a tasting where participants could feel a mild tingle from an untested ingredient. Put the steps for judging whether the risk is minimal in the correct order.

options.text: Identify the harms on the table, weigh their probability and severity, then consider the safeguards and context
Consider the safeguards first, then weigh probability and severity, then list the possible harms
options.misconception: Starts with the controls rather than the harms being controlled

options.text: List the possible harms, consider the safeguards, then weigh probability and severity
options.misconception: Places the safeguards before the judgement they inform

options.text: Weigh probability and severity first, then list the harms and only afterwards consider the safeguards
options.misconception: Judges the numbers before knowing what is being judged

questions.explanation: The judgement starts from the harms that could occur, then weighs their probability and severity, then asks what the context and safeguards do about them. Taking safeguards first or weighing numbers before naming harms reverses the order.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Value after a transform applied twice
questions.learningObjective: Determine the published code produced by a transform applied twice.

stimulus.body: A costing sheet records that dish codes are published by adding 4 to the raw code and keeping the last two digits. The rule is applied twice to every code before publication.

questions.stem: Given that note, what is the published code for a raw dish code of 78?

options.text: 86, because 78 becomes 82 and 82 becomes 86 when the rule is applied twice
82, because the rule is applied once and the second application only confirms it
options.misconception: Treats the second application as a confirmation step

options.text: 78, because adding 4 and keeping two digits leaves a two digit code unchanged
options.misconception: Believes the increment cannot alter a two digit value

options.text: 90, because the rule adds 4 to the code and then doubles it before trimming
options.misconception: Invents a doubling step that the note does not describe

questions.explanation: The rule runs twice on the running value, so 78 becomes 82 and 82 becomes 86, with the last two digits kept at each step. Applying it once, assuming an increment leaves two digits untouched, or adding a doubling step invents rules.
questions.hint: Apply the rule twice in sequence.

They can be left in place, because only seven per cent of the rows are unique
options.misconception: Treats a small proportion as evidence of safety

options.text: The whole sheet should be withheld, because any uniqueness at all disqualifies a file
options.misconception: Rules out every release that contains a single unique row

That the sheet's trials are reproducible, because a majority share is enough to support that

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a debriefing must achieve and why its timing matters.
questions.stem: The sheet records that suppliers were told a survey was about supplier reliability when it was really about tardiness. Explain what the debriefing owed to those suppliers must achieve and why the timing matters.

answer.exemplar: The debriefing must tell the suppliers that the survey's real topic was tardiness, explain why the stated topic was used, and offer them the choice to withdraw their answers, because consent was taken for a different question. Timing matters because the debriefing has to come while the participants can still change what happens with their data; if it is delayed until the results are published, the choice is no longer real and the deception has already shaped the analysis that was reported.

questions.explanation: The debriefing must disclose the real topic and restore the choice over the answers, and it must come while that choice still affects the study. A debriefing after publication cannot undo the deception, and results alone do not explain it.
questions.hint: Debrief while the choice still matters.

answer.exemplar: Taking a remainder means dividing and keeping what is left over, so 60 divided by 17 gives 9 with nothing further to carry, and 9 divided by 17 leaves 9 again because it is already smaller than the divisor. questions.learningObjective: Judge minimal risk and name the features that support the judgement.
questions.stem: The sheet describes a supervised knife skills session using the trainees own knives, with protective gear and vegetables only. First, state whether the risk is minimal and why; second, name the two features that most support that judgement.

options.text: Yes, it is minimal, because the activity is ordinary kitchen work and the safeguards make harm unlikely
Yes, it is minimal, because the session was supervised and no trainee was actually injured
options.misconception: Judges the risk only from the outcome rather than the procedure

options.text: No, it is not minimal, because using sharp knives is inherently a serious physical risk
options.misconception: Treats the presence of any hazard as automatically above minimal risk

options.text: Yes, it is minimal, because the session collected no personal data at all
options.misconception: Relies on data absence alone and ignores the physical activity

questions.explanation: The risk is minimal because the activity is ordinary kitchen work and the safeguards make harm unlikely, and those are the two features that matter. Supervision alone does not decide it, and data absence says nothing about physical risk.
questions.hint: Ordinary activity plus safeguards.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Value after a transform applied twice
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a published code produced by a transform applied twice.
questions.stem: On this sheet a transform adds 5 percent of itself and keeps a whole number, and the published code comes from two applications starting from 80. How should the published code be read?

options.text: As 88, because 80 becomes 84 and 84 becomes 88 once 88.2 is kept as a whole number
As 84, because the second application only confirms the first rounded result
options.misconception: Treats the second application as a confirmation step

options.text: As 84.5, because the whole number rule applies only after both applications
options.misconception: Defers the rounding to the end rather than each step

options.text: As 92, because five percent of a running value reads as about a fifth of it
options.misconception: Misreads five percent as a fifth

questions.explanation: Each application adds five percent and keeps a whole number, so 80 becomes 84 and 84 becomes 88 once 88.2 is trimmed. Confirming the first result, deferring the rule or reading five percent as a fifth gives a different figure.
questions.hint: Round after each application.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Assess what an archive held beyond its destruction date indicates.
questions.stem: The sheet gives 31 August 2024 as the destruction date for a supplier contract archive, and the archive was still in the safe at the 20 October 2026 review. What does that indicate?

options.text: Two full years of retention beyond the schedule, since 31 August 2026 preceded the review
Three years of retention beyond the schedule, because three calendar years were touched
options.misconception: Counts calendar years touched rather than completed anniversaries

options.text: Two and a half years of retention, because the exact elapsed time is the honest figure
options.misconception: Offers a fractional figure where the schedule counts whole years

options.text: No breach, because the archive was locked in a safe and could not be read
options.misconception: Treats physical security as if it satisfied a retention rule

questions.explanation: The second anniversary of 31 August 2024 fell on 31 August 2026, before the review, so two full years were retained beyond the schedule. Counting calendar years, using a fraction and noting the archive was locked all miss the rule.
questions.hint: Two completed anniversaries, not three.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Share of records unique on the quasi-identifiers
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage of bookings unique on a set of quasi-identifiers.
questions.stem: The sheet holds 200 event bookings and records that 20 of them are the only rows combining postcode, month and table size. What share of the rows is unique on that combination, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Twenty of two hundred is one tenth, so 10 per cent of the bookings are unique on the three quasi-identifiers and directly matchable. Calling a tenth negligible, or dividing 200 by 20, misreports the sheet.
questions.hint: One in ten rows.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Share of replications inside a stated interval
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a replication share supports and what it does not.
questions.stem: The sheet reports that 13 of 26 repeated costings were finished within the two-day window. Explain what that share supports and what it does not support about reproducibility.

answer.exemplar: Thirteen of twenty-six is 50 per cent, so half of the repeated costings finished inside the two-day window and half did not. The figure therefore supports a claim that the result can be reproduced inside the window for some attempts under some conditions, and it does not support a claim that the result reproduces generally, since the failures are not described and could share a single cause such as an ingredient that was out of stock on those days.

questions.explanation: Thirteen of twenty-six is 50 per cent, so it supports a claim of partial reproducibility inside the window, not a general one. Presenting half as most, or ignoring that the missing half may share one undescribed cause, misleads.
questions.hint: Half is partial, not general.
